To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) GMCs in our simulations are born with a typical mass of ∼105 M⊙, a typical size of ∼30 pc, and a lifetime of ∼10 Myr; (ii) GMCs form preferentially in regions where gas is converging; (iii) GMCs form in a hierarchical fashion, with the most massive ones forming from the merger of smaller clouds; (iv) GMCs form at a rate that is roughly proportional to the gas surface density;

the ISM of our galaxy is characterized by a large amount of molecular gas, that is distributed in GMCs of different masses, sizes and star formation rates, and that the interaction is not the main driver of star formation in the galaxy.
the star-forming gas is mostly controlled by feedback, and that the interaction with the M 51 companion galaxy is of secondary importance.

understanding the role of galactic dynamics and the interplay of different physical processes in determining the evolution of the star-formng ISM.
the role of the galactic environment in the formation and evolution of GMCs and the star formation process.
the formation and evolution of GMCs in a galactic environment, and how they are affected by the environment itself.

the interaction with the M51 companion is important, but not dominant, in determining the overall properties of the IS M in our simulated galaxy.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interaction is a necessary condition to form a galaxy like M51, but that it is not a sufficient one to explain the observed properties.

the ISM is a self-regulating system, where the star formation and feedback cycle drives the gas to a quasi-stationary state, and that the global properties of the ISMs are largely independent of the external perturbations.
the star-forming gas in the simulated galaxy is in a steady state, with a constant gas fraction and star formation rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while the interaction with a companion galaxy is important in generating cold gas, it is not a necessary condition to form stars.
the star-forming gas in our simulations is characterized by a power-law distribution of GMCs with a slope close to the observed value of -2, which is consistent with a turbulent origin.
the star formation process is a complex interplay of the local environment of a GMC and the large-scale properties of the galaxy.
